title: Pneumothorax -- Continuing Education Activity
content: A pneumothorax is a collection of air outside the lung but within the pleural cavity. It occurs when air accumulates between the parietal and visceral pleura inside the chest. The air accumulation can apply pressure on the lung and make it collapse. Pneumothoraces can be even further classified as simple, tension, or open. A simple pneumothorax does not shift the mediastinal structures, as does a tension pneumothorax. An open pneumothorax also is known as a "sucking" chest wound. This activity examines when this condition should be considered in differential diagnosis and how to evaluate it properly. This activity highlights the role of the interprofessional team in caring for patients with this condition.

title: Pneumothorax -- Introduction
content: A pneumothorax is a collection of air outside the lung but within the pleural cavity. It occurs when air accumulates between the parietal and visceral pleurae inside the chest. Air accumulation can exert pressure on the lung and cause collapse (see Image. Upper Lobe Pneumothorax). The degree of collapse determines the clinical presentation of pneumothorax (see Image. Right Tension Pneumothorax Radiograph). Air can enter the pleural space by 2 mechanisms: either through trauma that creates a communication channel through the chest wall or by rupture of the visceral pleura. There are 2 types of pneumothorax: traumatic and atraumatic. The 2 subtypes of atraumatic pneumothorax are primary and secondary. A primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) occurs automatically without a known eliciting event, while a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP) occurs after an underlying pulmonary disease. A traumatic pneumothorax can be the result of blunt or penetrating trauma. Pneumothoraces can be even further classified as simple, tension, or open. A simple pneumothorax does not shift the mediastinal structures, as does a tension pneumothorax (see Image . Left-Sided Tension Pneumothorax Radiograph). An open pneumothorax is an open wound in the chest wall through which air moves in and out. [1] [2] [3] [4]

title: Pneumothorax -- Epidemiology
content: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax typically occurs between the ages of 20 and 30. The incidence of PSP in the United States is 7 per 100,000 men and 1 per 100,000 women per year. [5] Most recurrences occur within the first year, and incidence ranges from 25% to 50%. The recurrence rate is highest over the first 30 days. Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax is seen more in older patients, 60-65 years. The incidence of SSP is 6.3 cases per 100,000 patients, with 2 cases in men and 2 in women. The male-to-female ratio is 3:1. COPD accounts for 26 pneumothoraces per 100,000 patients. [6] The risk of spontaneous pneumothorax in heavy smokers is 102 times higher than in non-smokers.

title: Pneumothorax -- Epidemiology
content: The leading cause of iatrogenic pneumothorax is transthoracic needle aspiration (usually for biopsies), and the second leading cause is central venous catheterization. These occur more frequently than spontaneous pneumothorax, and their number increases as intensive care modalities advance. The incidence of iatrogenic pneumothorax is 5 per 10,000 admissions in the hospital.

title: Pneumothorax -- Epidemiology
content: The incidence of tension pneumothorax is challenging to determine, as one-third of cases in trauma centers have decompressive needle thoracostomies before reaching the hospital, and not all of these had tension pneumothorax. Pneumomediastinum has an incidence of 1 case per 10,000 hospital admissions.

title: Pneumothorax -- Pathophysiology
content: The pressure gradient inside the thorax changes with a pneumothorax. Usually, the pressure in the pleural space is negative relative to atmospheric pressure. When the chest wall expands outwards, the lung also expands outwards due to surface tension between the parietal and visceral pleurae. Lungs tend to collapse due to elastic recoil. When communication occurs between the alveoli and the pleural space, air fills the pleural space, altering the pressure gradient; lung collapse, unit equilibrium is achieved, or the rupture is sealed. Pneumothorax enlarges, reducing vital capacity and oxygen partial pressure. Clinical presentation of a pneumothorax can range from asymptomatic to chest pain and shortness of breath. A tension pneumothorax can cause severe hypotension (obstructive shock) and even death. Increased central venous pressure can result in distended neck veins and hypotension. Patients may have tachypnea, dyspnea, tachycardia, and hypoxia.

title: Pneumothorax -- Pathophysiology
content: In most patients, spontaneous pneumothorax results from rupture of bullae or blebs. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax is defined as occurring in patients without underlying lung disease, but these patients had asymptomatic bullae or blebs on thoracotomy. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in tall, thin young people due to increased shear forces or more negative pressure at the lung apex. Lung inflammation and oxidative stress are essential to the pathogenesis of primary spontaneous pneumothorax. Current smokers have increased inflammatory cells in small airways and are at increased risk of pneumothorax.

title: Pneumothorax -- Pathophysiology
content: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in the presence of underlying lung disease, primarily chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; others may include tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, cystic fibrosis, malignancy, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, and pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia. Iatrogenic pneumothorax occurs due to a complication of a medical or surgical procedure. Thoracentesis is the most common cause. Traumatic pneumothoraces can result from blunt or penetrating trauma; these often create a 1-way valve in the pleural space (letting the airflow in but not flow out) and hence hemodynamic compromise. Tension pneumothorax most commonly occurs in the ICU among positive-pressure-ventilated patients.

title: Pneumothorax -- History and Physical
content: In primary spontaneous pneumothorax, patients are typically minimally symptomatic because otherwise healthy individuals tolerate the physiologic consequences well. The most common symptoms are chest pain and shortness of breath. The chest pain is pleuritic, sharp, severe, and radiates to the ipsilateral shoulder. In SSP, dyspnea is more pronounced due to reduced underlying lung reserve. A history of pneumothorax is essential, as recurrence occurs in 15-40% of cases. Recurrence on the contralateral side can also occur. On examination, the following findings are noted: Respiratory discomfort Increased respiratory rate Asymmetrical lung expansion Decreased tactile fremitus Hyperresonant percussion note Decreased intensity of breath sounds or absent breath sounds In tension pneumothorax, the following additional findings are seen: Tachycardia of more than 134 beats per minute Hypotension Jugular venous distension Cyanosis Respiratory failure Cardiac arrest

title: Pneumothorax -- History and Physical
content: Some traumatic pneumothoraces are associated with subcutaneous emphysema. Pneumothorax may be difficult to diagnose from a physical exam, especially in a noisy trauma bay. However, it is essential to make the diagnosis of tension pneumothorax on a physical exam.

title: Pneumothorax -- Evaluation
content: Chest radiography, ultrasonography, or computed tomography can be used for diagnosis, although chest radiography is more commonly used. Radiographic findings of a 2.5 cm air space are equivalent to a 30% pneumothorax. Computed tomography may diagnose occult pneumothoraces, but they are usually clinically insignificant. The extended focused abdominal sonography for trauma (E-FAST) exam has been a more recent diagnostic tool for pneumothorax. The absence usually indicates lung sliding, the absence of a comet-tail artifact, and the presence of a lung point. Unfortunately, this diagnostic method is highly operator-dependent, and sensitivity and specificity can vary. In skilled hands, ultrasonography has up to a 94% sensitivity and 100% specificity (better than a chest x-ray). If a patient is hemodynamically unstable with suspected tension pneumothorax, intervention is not withheld to await imaging (see Image. Portable Chest Radiograph, Left Deep Sulcus Pneumothorax). Needle decompression can be performed if the patient is hemodynamically unstable, with a convincing history and physical examination consistent with tension pneumothorax. [7] [8] [9] [10] [11]

title: Pneumothorax -- Treatment / Management
content: Management depends on the clinical scenario. For patients with associated symptoms and showing signs of instability, needle decompression is the treatment of a pneumothorax. This is usually performed with a 14- to 16-gauge and 4.5 cm in length angiocatheter, just superior to the rib in the second intercostal space in the midclavicular line. After needle decompression or in cases of stable pneumothoraces, the treatment is to insert a thoracostomy tube. This is usually placed above the rib in the fifth intercostal space, anterior to the midaxillary line. The size of the thoracostomy tube is usually determined by the patient's height and weight and by the presence of an associated hemothorax. Open "sucking" chest wounds are treated initially with a 3-sided occlusive dressing. Further treatment may require tube thoracostomy and repair of the chest wall defect.

title: Pneumothorax -- Treatment / Management
content: In an asymptomatic small primary spontaneous pneumothorax (depth <2 cm), the patient is usually discharged for outpatient follow-up after 2-4 weeks. If the patient is symptomatic or the depth or size exceeds 2 cm, needle aspiration is performed. After aspiration, if the patient improves and the residual depth is less than 2 cm, the patient is discharged; otherwise, tube thoracostomy is performed.

title: Pneumothorax -- Treatment / Management
content: In secondary spontaneous pneumothorax, if the pneumothorax is less than 1 cm in size or depth and there is no dyspnea, the patient is admitted, high-flow oxygen is administered, and observation is performed for 24 hours. If the size/depth is between 1-2 cm, needle aspiration is done, then the residual size of pneumothorax is seen; if the depth after the needle aspiration is less than 1 cm, management is done with oxygen inhalation and observation, and in case of more than 2 cm, tube thoracostomy is done. If the depth exceeds 2 cm or there is breathlessness, a tube thoracostomy is performed.

title: Pneumothorax -- Treatment / Management
content: Air can be reabsorbed from the pleural space at a rate of 1.5% per day. Using supplemental oxygen can increase this reabsorption rate. Increasing the inspired oxygen fraction displaces nitrogen from atmospheric air, altering the pressure gradient between the pleural space and the capillaries. Pneumothorax on chest radiography, approximately 25% or larger, usually requires needle aspiration if symptomatic; if this fails, tube thoracostomy is performed. Indications for surgical intervention (VATS vs thoracotomy): Continuous air leak for longer than 7 days Bilateral pneumothoraces The first episode in high-risk profession patients, ie, divers, pilots Recurrent ipsilateral pneumothorax Contralateral pneumothorax Patients who have AIDS

title: Pneumothorax -- Treatment / Management
content: Patients undergoing video-assisted thoracic surgery (VATS) get pleurodesis to occlude the pleural space. Mechanical pleurodesis with bleb/bullectomy decreases the recurrence rate of pneumothorax to <5%. Options for mechanical pleurodesis include stripping the parietal pleura versus using an abrasive "scratchpad" or dry gauze. A chemical pleurodesis is an option for patients who may not tolerate mechanical pleurodesis. Options for chemical pleurodesis include talc, tetracycline, doxycycline, and minocycline, all of which irritate the pleural lining.

title: Pneumothorax -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Differential diagnoses of pneumothorax include: Aspiration, bacterial or viral pneumonia Acute aortic dissection Myocardial infarction Pulmonary embolism Acute pericarditis Esophageal spasm Esophageal rupture Rib fracture Diaphragmatic injuries

title: Pneumothorax -- Prognosis
content: PSP is usually benign and typically resolves spontaneously without significant intervention. Recurrence can occur for up to 3 years. The 5-year recurrence rate is 30% for PSP and 43% for SSP. The risk of recurrence increases with each subsequent pneumothorax: 30% with the first, 40% after a second, and more than 50% after the third recurrence. PSP is not considered a significant health threat, but deaths have been reported. SSPs are more lethal depending on the underlying lung disease and the size of the pneumothorax. Patients with COPD and HIV have high mortality after pneumothorax. The mortality of SSP is 10%. Mortality of tension pneumothorax is high if appropriate measures are not taken.

title: Pneumothorax -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patients with pneumothorax should be educated that they should not travel by air or to remote areas until after the complete resolution of the pneumothorax. Patients with high-risk occupations like scuba divers and pilots should be advised not to dive or fly until definitive surgical management of their pneumothorax is done. All patients are advised to stop smoking. They should be assessed for desire to quit smoking; they should be educated and provided with pharmacotherapy if they decide to quit.

title: Pneumothorax -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Do not let a chest radiograph or computed tomography scan delay treatment with needle decompression or thoracostomy tube if the patient is clinically unstable, ie, tension pneumothorax. Worsening subcutaneous emphysema may be associated with malposition of a chest tube; repositioning with a new chest tube is recommended. A chest tube should never be reinserted, as this can increase the patient's risk for empyema. An untreated pneumothorax is a contraindication for flying or scuba diving. If air transport is required, a thoracostomy tube should be placed before transport. If there is a persistent or recurrent pneumothorax despite treatment with a thoracostomy tube, these patients need specialty consultations for a possible video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) with or without pleurodesis or thoracotomy. If the patient is discharged from the hospital after a resolved pneumothorax, recommendations should be made against flying or scuba diving for at least 2 weeks. Patients with a known history of spontaneous pneumothorax should not be medically cleared for occupations involving flying or scuba diving.

title: Pneumothorax -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The emergency department physician often manages pneumothorax. In some cases, the disorder may be managed by the ICU staff and the thoracic surgeon. The nurse cares for patients with chest tubes. All nurses who manage patients with chest tubes should understand how a chest drain functions. Patients require examination on every shift, and chest tube patency is important. Patients with small pneumothorax can be observed if they have no symptoms. If discharged, the patient should be seen within 24 hours.
